title: Judith
lead: The widow of Bethulia who, in the book that bears her name, beheads the Assyrian general Holofernes and saves Israel. The book is in the Old Testament of Catholic and Orthodox Christians and among the Apocrypha for Protestants; it is not in the Jewish Bible, though medieval Jews linked her story with Hanukkah.

sections.b: Judith is a pious, rich and beautiful widow who rebukes the elders of her besieged town for setting God a deadline, prays, goes into the enemy camp, and kills its general (Judith 8–13). The book draws her from Israel's earlier heroines: Jael, who killed Sisera in her tent (Judges 4:17–22), Deborah and Miriam, who led songs of victory (Judges 5; Exodus 15:20–21), and Esther, who risked herself before a foreign king. The earliest Christian mention, 1 Clement 55, praises her courage. Catholic liturgy applies her praises to Mary (Judith 13:18; Judith 15:9–10), and medieval Jews retold her story at Hanukkah. Protestant readers have praised her courage and questioned her deceit (Judith 9:10; Judith 11:5–19). Whether her story is history or a story told to teach is debated; most scholars read it as the second.
